newsitem.title: UK: Wary UK funds say strategy intact after poll rout.
newsitem.headline: Wary UK funds say strategy intact after poll rout.

text.p: UK fund managers will keep a wary eye on Labour Party policy after its landslide victory in the British election, but do not plan any immediate changes in investment strategy.

They told Reuters on Friday that the size of the Labour majority, expected to be about 180 seats, had come as a surprise and did raise concerns that the party could stray from its relatively strict policy plans.

"Does it change our investment policy from what it was last night? I don't think it does on the basis of what I have heard so far," said Peter Jones, chief executive of Friends Provident Asset Management.
"I shall have some anxieties but I don't propose doing anything about."
Industry players said any escalation of worries about Labour policy could see some asset allocation shifts, with cash, overseas equities and fixed income seen benefiting.
"We know the direction that Labour has indicated. That is much easier for a fund manager than an uncertain indication," said Elizabeth Thom, head of UK equities at Edinburgh Fund Managers.
But the key factor affecting investment strategy remained U.S. market direction, they said.

"The thing that matters is what happens on Wall Street. We are the 51st state of the U.S.. Wall Street will drive the levels of the valuations just like it has for the last several years," said one senior UK fund manager who asked not to be named.

Mike Grimble, chief strategist at Norwich Union Investment Management, said he would closely watch Tony Blair's ability to maintain control of the party with the larger than expected majority, but was not making any early allocation changes.
"We are keeping a wary eye open and considering increasing cash weightings but the trigger will probably be more from the U.S. We are a cautious investor at the moment rather than a raging bull."

Friends' Jones said possible changes to advance corporation tax (ACT) would be a major factor. Under current legislation, pension funds are allowed to claim back ACT on dividends and Labour is expected to scale back or scrap this tax relief.
But he said current talk was that it would be changed at the end of the year rather than June or July, and that the change would be phased in over three years.
"I think that is the sort of thing that the market probably could come to terms with."
"Old labour government's would have had no concern about destabilising stock markets. This one, arguably, may have a different view of things," said Jones.
He said possible allocation changes if concerns grew were a move into overseas equities, or UK index-linked bonds.
Norwich Union's Grimble said the outlook for bonds was likely to improve because the tax take under labour would increase and at least initially spending would be tight.
"We expect some volatility...but as long as the right noises come out of Tony Blair's office, then the market will take it in its stride," he said.

ING Barings' global investment strategist Matthew Merritt said the equity market was likely to be most affected by the Labour win due to fears about ACT changes and the effect that could have on pension fund investors.
But gilts, he said, could "only stack up very well in value terms. Any near term vulnerability can only be an opportunity to build exposure there."
-- Andrew Gill, London newsroom +171 542 5887
